notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0128b.stoa003.opp-l: Line 3: several evident scanning errors corrected silently (didimus = dicimus, illius = filius, telatio = relatio, orat = erat, Selh = Seth). Line 4: the objection is obscure and possibly corrupt; 'Et quam (al. quasi) nemo, dixit Scriptura, qui enarret?' is rendered tentatively, and the final sentence ('ut dicant se posse nosse... non autem ignorabilis') reads more like the Catholic position than the Arian one, so its sense is uncertain. Line 5: the citation 'John 14:17' is as printed; the verse is John 14:7.

Line 1 opens with a damaged phrase, 'non a. tur'; a verb such as 'fallitur' or 'erratur' is presumably meant, rendered '[deceived]'. Several scriptural references in the edition are misprinted and have been corrected in the translation: Prov. VII, 23-26 to Prov. 8:23-25; Rom. VII to Rom. 8; Col. 1:16 to Col. 1:15; Acts XIII, 52 to Acts 13:32-33. In line 2, 'cujus JX' is corrupt; a word such as 'sermo' is presumably meant and is supplied as '[address]'. The final clause ('ne apud Salvatorem... deitatem') is awkward Latin and is translated literally.

Objection numbered 'i' is evidently 4 (scan error). The text of Objection 5 is confused and probably corrupt; translated as nearly literally as possible. 'paterni hominis' in the final sentence read as 'paterni nominis', as earlier in the passage. Jer. 9:10 'vocem substantiae meae' follows this text's Old Latin form (Vulgate differs). Isa. 6 reference given as 6:3 (edition prints 6:5).

Objection 6 and 7 are obscure and ungrammatical in the Latin, as transmitted; translated as literally as sense allows. In line 13 'Mei' read as 'fidei'; 'personat!' as 'personae'. The scriptural reference given as John 14:12 is John 14:10-11; 1 Thess. 5:45 is 5:4-5. 'Triusianos' is Fulgentius's coinage (adherents of three substances).

Objection 9: the Arian text is garbled and its syntax hard to construe ('cum ipsa anto scriptio ostendat', 'ut manifestaret ipsam esse et propheta dicendo', 'et splendidum contigit'); 'anto' read as 'ante'; translation is tentative. The psalm cited (Ex utero ante luciferum genui te) is Ps. 109:3 (Vulgate), not 'CII, 5' as printed. Objection 10: 'Nunquid non occurrit beneficii munus, quando unus non est cum duobus designatus' is obscure and rendered literally. Psalm 'XCVI, 8' and Rom. citation numbers kept as printed where unclear; the 'Moses' quotation (Laetamini caeli...) is in fact Deut. 32:43 (LXX), though the edition cites a psalm.

Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'Deris' for 'Deus', 'onicio' read as 'officio', 'conlitetur' for 'confitetur', 'Sanctuiu' for 'Sanctum'). The Isaiah quotation 'Domine, praeter te alium non novimus' is read with 'alium' for 'altum' (Isa. 26:13). 'Unum ... esse nec inter se' reflects a slightly disordered phrase in the text. The Johannine Comma (1 John 5:7) is quoted as Fulgentius gives it.

nodes.text: The Book of St Fulgentius against the Arians, containing ten responses to ten objections.

It has been said that the Father begot the Son ineffably from himself, that is, from that which he himself is. It has been added that [the Son] was born not from outside, but from God. These [statements] need no response, because they agree with our faith.

First objection. What is said to this? If he was born from God, he is from within God; but if he is not from within, neither is he from him. If different words are merely set down, what use is that, if the truth itself is not professed?

Response. Indeed, when Father and Son are named, a difference of words is recognised in these two names; yet rather, through these two different words the one nature of both is signified, since the difference of these names does not divide natures but shows the truth of the begetting, so that we may recognise that from one true Father one true Son has come forth. And thus, when the true begetting by the Father and the true birth of the Son are proclaimed, in the one who begets and the one begotten not only the unity of substance but also, in each one, the distinctness of person can be recognised, so that neither is he who begot thought to have been born, nor is he who was born thought to be anything other than he who begot. For the Father is not the same [person] as the Son, since in each the distinctness of the persons is preserved; but what the Father is, that the Son also is, because the Son was born God from God, perfect from perfect, immeasurable from immeasurable, almighty from almighty, coeternal from the eternal Father, as the Truth himself says: All things that the Father has are mine (John 17:10). Father and Son, then, are relative names, which do not separate the nature of the one begetting and the one begotten, but without doubt signify one [nature]. We call that relative which we refer to the recognising of another, so that when we name one we point to the other: as among human beings these relative terms are often named, father and son, son and father, father-in-law and son-in-law, son-in-law and father-in-law. For one is called father so that he may be known to have begotten a son, and [the other] is called son so that he may be shown to have been begotten by a father. Nor in this difference of names is a difference of natures found, since each is alike called a man, although one is called father and the other son. Indeed, the one nature of father and son could not be recognised if these were not different words; for if both were called fathers, they would certainly be unlike in nature: each would exist from himself and would not have a common substance with the other, nor would there be one deity for those who had not one nature. And it would follow that the two fathers would beget two sons, since unless a true offspring came forth from each, the truth of the name of father would appear in neither. Now in the case of two sons born of different fathers, even though there might be no difference of relative name, let it be considered whether there could be a common nature. Who does not see that in each the name of son is one, but that the nature of both is not one? Rather, each son has a common nature not with the other son, with whom he had one name of relation, but with the father from whom he came forth. But why argue further about two fathers and two sons, when the truth of this assertion does not need a plurality of persons, but can more easily be supported, as proof of itself, by considering one man? By this it may be recognised that relative names, by their difference, do not show a difference of natures, but pertain chiefly to signifying the persons, so that, namely, when one is shown, the person of the other is also known; and that the name which is always common to father and son is not the one by which the personal relation is shown, but the one by which the substantial property is pointed out. Was not Seth, born of his father Adam, and begotten of one who was not begotten, called the son of his father Adam? Until he reached manhood, so as to beget a son, he could not be called father; and before he begot, he was only a son; but when he begot, he then began also to be a father. So when the different name of father was added, no difference of nature was produced in him; and when one man had begun to have these two words, his nature was not changed, or divided, or doubled in him. For he was a son, because he came forth from a father; he was a father, because he begot a son. Yet he did not so have the nature of a son, in which he was born, that remaining in it he could not be a father; nor did he acquire another essence along with the name of father, so as to lose the substance of a son in which he had been born. But, as is true, just as he was a man when he came into being as a son by being born, so he remained a man when he became a father by begetting; nor was he anything other than a man, which Adam, from whom he himself was born, was, and which Enos, who was begotten from him, was. So in God the Father and God the Son, with the distinctness of persons preserved, let that not be called impossible which is proved even by the example of any man whatever; but let us distinguish what is known to pertain to relation and what to substance. Father and Son are names of relation; but the name of substance is one, which is called God. The names of relation, then, each holds singly; but the name of substance they possess as one in common, because, although one is called Father and the other Son, yet the Son is God just as the Father is God: for by those two names a true begetting is recognised, but by this one common name the unity of substance is shown.

Objection 2. We do not recall ever having read the things put forward above, because it is written of him: Who will tell his generation? (Isa. 53). And [is it] as if (another reading: as though) Scripture said 'no one' who might tell it? These men must be challenged to say that they can know [it], since his generation is untellable, but not unknowable.

Response. It is written: I believed, therefore I have spoken; and we believe, therefore we speak (2 Cor. 4:13); and we confidently profess that the generation of the Son is untellable, [but] not unknowable. For it does not follow that what cannot be told cannot be known, since no one is able to tell God himself, and yet no one may be ignorant of him with impunity. Indeed, God is so far knowable, though he is untellable, that the blessed Apostle declares certain people inexcusable on this account, because when they had known God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks (Rom. 1:21). For if the Lord did not wish to be known by us, he would not have said: If you had known me, you would surely have known my Father also (John 14:17). Nor would he have rebuked Philip, when he said, Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us, with this reproach, saying: I have been with you so long a time, and you have not known me; Philip, he who has seen me has seen the Father also. For by this word the Lord wished to show that all that was sought was found in him: for it cannot be that the Son, in whom the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily (Col. 2:9), has anything less than the everlasting and immeasurable Father. God, then, is not unknowable, though he is untellable; but he is known by the faithful so that he may be loved, although he is told neither by human tongues nor by angelic ones. For the apostle Paul shows that ignorance of God is nothing other than slavery to demons, saying: But then indeed, not knowing God, you served those who by nature are not gods (Gal. 4:9). Just as we must not be ignorant of the divinity of Christ, though we cannot tell it, so too, although no one has the means to tell his birth, knowledge of it is not taken away from the faithful. For who would proclaim one born whose birth he did not know? Who would call him Son and not know him begotten? Who could believe in a Father whom he did not consider to have begotten? The Father truly begot, and the Son was truly born. It is given to us, then, to know the true birth of the Son, although it is not given [to us] to tell how he was born. For the prophet too did not say, But who has known his generation, but, who has told it? (Isa. 53:8). Therefore we worthily know the divine generation, as far as is lawful for a man, in this: when we both call the generation true and proclaim that the generation itself, which is true, is untellable. So the Son is recognised as truly born of the Father's substance, when his birth, which is from the untellable God, is proclaimed untellable: for the true birth of the Son is beyond doubt untellable, because he has one substance with his untellable begetter.

Objection 3. It is right to profess his generation in the way the Lord himself says through the Scriptures: The Lord created me the beginning of his ways, before the ages he established me (Prov. 8:22). And it continues: And before all the hills he begot me. And again: I came forth from the Father and have come into this world (John 16:29). And again: The Lord said to me, You are my Son, today I have begotten you (Ps. 2:7). And after he was known in the flesh, the evangelist professes of him, saying: And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). And the Apostle says: Who is the Firstborn of all creation (Col. 1:15). See, we profess [him] created, established and begotten, without any irrational ambiguity.

Reply. In both births of Christ he is not [deceived] who professes in Christ, Son of God and of man, both full divinity from the Father and full manhood from the mother; and so recognises that each substance in him is true, provided he distinguishes with faithful devotion what befits eternity and what befits time. For we must not be ignorant that the one who, without beginning, as creator according to the divinity, was begotten of the Father, was himself created in time from a human being according to the flesh. For in that birth, which has no beginning, the majesty of everlasting divinity is recognised; but in this one the loving-kindness of everlasting divinity is found. For he who, not created but creator, begotten of the creator, had by his goodness created man, was himself afterwards by his loving-kindness created from man. Nor did he disdain to become his own work, so that through him the state of his work might be restored. Wisdom, then, wishing to foretell the mystery of this creation, so as to show the future sacrament of its Incarnation, in the prophetic manner, by which future things are usually narrated under the expression of past time, said: The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works (Prov. 8:22). It shows the cause of the creation when it does not keep silent that it was created the beginning of God's ways, for his works. For, to show that what it says was created belongs not to that eternal birth but to this time, in which the Son of God is found to have taken up flesh, let attention be paid to what it put first: If I announce to you (it says) the things that happen daily, I shall remember to declare the things that are from the age (ibid. 21). So, since these things were happening daily, it forewarns that things done from the age are being announced, [and] shows that what it is about to tell us belongs not to eternity but to time. For this reason it at once added: The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works. That wisdom was created, then, is not before the ages but from the age. And that the Son was created as the beginning of ways, what else is it but that he himself was made the way for us, so that, with him as leader and guide, through the grace of adoption which we have received, entry might lie open to us by divine gift to progress in virtues? That this may appear more clearly, we must observe that the Son was made the beginning of creation for this: not to found a new creation again, but to renew [the creation] long since lost through oldness (another reading: the oldness; another: the old [creation]). For the apostles too are found to have been made the beginning of this creation, through whose office he restored what had collapsed before, as blessed James says of God the Father: Willingly he begot us by the Word of truth, that we might be a certain beginning of his creation (Jas. 1:18). It is therefore shown by the clearest indications that the creation in this place is to be referred not to the founding of all creatures but to the restoration of men: just as holy David also prayed when he was terrified by the remembrance of a twofold crime, not only of a violated marriage but also of an innocent husband slain. So while he was thinking to wash away the stain of so great a deed with a river of tears, he poured out this among the groans which he had as witnesses of his sorrow: Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit in my inward parts (Ps. 50:12). He signified that to have a clean heart created in him was the same as to have a right spirit renewed in his inward parts. Christ, then, willed to be created for this, and his apostles to be made the beginning of this creation, so that through him man, who had perished through oldness, might be renewed. But wisdom said it was established before the age, to show that its birth, by which it was born of the Father, is unchangeable: for what is said to be established is in no way uprooted, and what is not uprooted is not changed. And so that the birth of his divinity may be recognised as without beginning, attention must be paid to what follows: Before he made the earth, before he set the depths, before the springs of waters came forth, before the mountains were settled, and before all the hills he begot me (Prov. 8:23-25). When this 'before' is said, absolutely every beginning is anticipated. This must be considered: that wherever that divine and eternal birth of the Son is shown, it is not said when he was born, but 'before' is always set down, so that whatever of infinity and eternity a man may wish to think, the birth of the Son is always to be thought of as before everything conceived in thought; and thus the birth of the Son of God may be recognised as without beginning, in which nothing is ever found but 'before' set down. But we should like to be answered: is what is begotten the same as what is created? If both are thought to be one, then let the world be said to be begotten by God, by whom it cannot be begotten, and [yet] was created. Let unbelieving men, too, be called sons of God, who have not been freed from the power of darkness; let those be called heirs of future blessedness who do not receive the faith of the Saviour. But if, as is true, to be created is one thing and to be begotten another, let it be distinguished in which substance Christ is said to be created by God, and in which he is proclaimed begotten of the Father. For the very passage of Scripture shows quite easily to those who inquire in which nature Christ is to be called created: namely in that in which he names [him] Lord, to show in himself the reality of the form of a servant, just as he also speaks in the psalm, saying: O Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid (Ps. 115:16). So he who was begotten of the Father as Lord was born of a handmaid as a servant. Because of the form of a servant, then, he said: The Lord created me; he says he was created not by the Father but by the Lord. For where he is said to be begotten according to the divinity, the Father is at once named, as he himself truly said: I came forth from the Father, and have come (John 8:42); and the blessed evangelist of him: And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father (John 1:14). You see that he did not say here 'from the Lord', but 'from the Father'. And as for the Apostle calling him the Firstborn of all creation (Col. 1:15), the creation is certainly understood as restored, not founded: the creation of the sons of God, by which from his servants they were made his brothers, who, according to the Apostle's word, is not ashamed to call us brothers, saying: I will tell your name to my brothers, in the midst of the Church I will praise you. And again: I will trust in him. And again: Behold, I and the children whom God has given me. Since, then, the children have shared in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same, that through death he might destroy him who had the dominion of death, that is, the devil; that he might free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery all their life. For nowhere does he take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Hence he had to be made like his brothers in all things, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people. For in that he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted (Heb. 2:11-18). We hear that Christ has brothers, we hear of the seed of Abraham; we hear [of him] destroying through death him who had the dominion of death; we hear [he was] tempted; we hear [he] suffered; and do we hesitate to profess Christ the Firstborn of all creation according to the mystery of the Incarnation? Since again the blessed Apostle shows by the testimony of his preaching in what respect we ought to take him as Firstborn, saying: We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who according to [his] purpose are called saints. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the Firstborn among many brothers (Rom. 8:28-29). So he who according to the deity was always Only-begotten without brothers was made according to the man the Firstborn among many brothers. This is taught more clearly again by that testimony of the Apostle where he is named Firstborn from the dead (Col. 1:18). For what is Firstborn from the dead but the man Christ Jesus, the first from among sinful men, exalted into the Son of God? But he was born, not a sinner from sinners as he was a man from men, but he was born a man, taken up by God without any sin, so that he might reconcile sinful men to God, freed from all sin. Such a man indeed had to be taken up by God, through whom men could be joined to God by free justification. He is therefore the Firstborn of all creation (Col. 1:15), assuredly of that [creation] of which we heard the blessed apostle James say a little before: Willingly he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be a certain beginning of his creation (Jas. 1:18). Of this creation the apostle Paul also says: If, then, there is any new creation in Christ (2 Cor. 5:17). Of which David too had foretold: Send forth your Spirit and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth (Ps. 103:30). Otherwise, if Christ is taken as Firstborn of all creation according to the divine birth, by what testimonies is he shown to be Firstborn from the dead before all creation, since those could not be called dead who had not yet even been created? We recognise Christ, then, as Only-begotten from the Father; let us profess (another reading: we profess) [him] Firstborn from the virgin. For in that birth he is truly Only-begotten, in which without beginning God alone was born of God alone; but in this birth he is the Firstborn of all creation (Col. 1:15), that is, of those whom he has deigned to adopt as brothers to himself through faith. But as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name (John 1:12). This generation is recognised as proclaimed in the second psalm too, where Christ, in the person of the man taken up, says: The Lord said to me, You are my Son, today I have begotten you (Ps. 2:7). To show that this was said according to the mystery of the future Incarnation, he added: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession. For how, according to the form of God, would he ask for the ends of the earth to possess, when he promises and gives to his faithful the kingdom of heaven, which is greater? He, then, who, remaining in the form of God, was made a servant for the salvation of servants, asked according to the form of a servant for the ends of the earth, so as to receive the nations as inheritance and possession, he who according to the divine nature, just as he made with the Father all things that are in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, so with the Father always possessed all things. That this generation which the second psalm suggests belongs to the mystery of the Incarnation, the book of the Acts of the Apostles testifies, when Paul speaks in the synagogue; whose [address] to the Jews is found to be of this kind: And we announce to you that promise which was made to our fathers, that God has fulfilled it for our children, raising up Jesus; as it is also written in the second psalm: You are my Son, today I have begotten you (Acts 13:32-33). So the Apostle shows that what the psalm said was said to the Son in respect of that in which he proclaims him raised from the dead. Let it be observed, then, which nature rose from the dead in Christ, and it will be understood in what respect Christ, begotten today, received the ends of the earth to possess. Let the distinctness of each nature in Christ therefore be recognised, so that he may be understood without error as created, established and begotten: he is begotten and established in that he was born untellably as Lord from the Lord; but created according to the human generation by which he was born a servant from a handmaid, so that him whom the Father alone begot before all things by nature, he might beget by grace for our salvation. Therefore we must recognise both natures in Christ the Lord, so that we may neither seem proud against the creator nor prove (another reading: be thought) ungrateful for the benefit of our Saviour, lest he deny himself before the Saviour the salvation which he seeks who denies the true deity of the Creator from God the Father.

Objection 4. But let those who presume, without reason, to say that the Son was born from the substance of the Father show, nevertheless, from the Scriptures how it is not a false profession of error when one who says that his generation is untellable asserts that he was born from the substance of the Father.

Answer. A failure of assertion is recognised when someone strives to destroy the rule of another's faith in such a way that he is unwilling to put forward a firm statement of his own belief. We, then, believe and confess the Son of God born from the substance of the Father, that is, from that which the Father is. For whatever is not the substance of God we cannot either adore or worship as God, observing with great care the precept of the law in which it is said: Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord. And: You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve (Deut. 6:4, 13). This God we believe to be not the Father alone, but the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For our faith, by which we worship and fear one God, is neither contracted by a personal union nor disjoined by a difference of substance: lest we either worship gods in the manner of the pagans by worshipping different substances, or deny the Son and the Spirit with Sabellius, not preserving the persons in the Trinity. The right belief of this faith is conveyed to us in truth not only by prophetic but also by apostolic teaching. For when Isaiah (another reading: Isaiah) was made worthy of the vision of God, the belief of this faith was made known to him, as the two seraphim cried three times: Holy, holy, holy (Isa. 6:3); and added once: Lord God of Sabaoth. Why is Holy said three times, if the person in the Godhead is not threefold? Why is Lord God said once, if the substance in the Godhead is not one? The Lord too, wishing to bless the people through Moses, commanded the form in which they were to be blessed, saying: Thus you shall bless my people, and I will bless them. May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine upon you and have mercy on you. May the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace (Num. 6:23-26). Lord is said three times, and always one Lord is named, so that in the Trinity, which is the true God, neither is the distinctness of the persons confounded nor the unity of substance denied. David also, pleasing to God in all things, in this belief prays in these words that the grace of the divine blessing may be poured upon the faithful people: May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him (Ps. 66:7-8). With this statement the blessed Apostle agrees, who, when in one place he had said: One God the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him (1 Cor. 8:6), and of the Holy Spirit also said: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption (Eph. 4:30); remembering that he had said 'from the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit', in order to show that this Trinity is one God, he says in another place: For from him, and through him, and in him are all things. And what he added in the singular: to him be glory for ages of ages (Rom. 11:36). That the Son was born from the substance of the Father both the Christian faith rightly proclaims and holy Scripture records: Paul the apostle says of the Son of God: Who, since he is the radiance of glory and the image of his substance (Heb. 1:3). Again the Lord says to Jeremiah: Take up a lament over the mountains, and men have not heard the voice of my substance, from the birds of the sky to the cattle (Jer. 9:10). And that the Son is the substance of the Father, the book of Wisdom plainly shows, saying: With the food of angels you nourished your people, you provided them bread prepared from heaven without labour, having in it every delight and every savour of sweetness: for you showed your substance and your sweetness which you have towards your children (Wis. 16:20-21). Scripture testifies that the bread given from heaven is the substance and sweetness of God: and that the bread truly given from heaven is the Son of God is shown by the words of the Son himself, who says: I am the living bread, who came down from heaven (John 6:41). Of which David says: Man ate the bread of angels (Ps. 77:25). See, that the Son came forth from the substance of the Father we not only believe on reasonable grounds, but also prove by testimonies, as Scripture says: Whoever loves the begetter loves him who was born of him (1 John 5:1); for true faith is not ignorant of what it believes, even if it cannot yet see what it hopes for and believes. But those who deny that the Son was born from the substance of the Father ought certainly to say from what they think the Son of God came forth: whether from nothing, or from something? If he came forth from nothing, he must be called a creation, not the creator. But if he is said [to have come] from something, then God also made that very thing from which he begot the Son. Or is he perhaps said to have had something coeternal from which he could beget the Son? If something coeternal is supposed from which the Son is believed to have been begotten, the error of the Manichaeans is confirmed by this assertion. But if there was nothing from which the Son was begotten, and yet he is not said to have been born from the substance of the Father, it remains that those who strive to proclaim him lesser in divinity plainly confess that the Son of God came forth from nothing. But perhaps it is said that the Son was born from the will of the Father: let it be said, then, whether the Father begot the Son from himself or from elsewhere? For if he begot him from himself, will could not precede the begetting, because it is wicked to believe that anything which did not always exist has newly befallen God. From this it is known that God made every creation from nothing by his will, but begot the Son by substance or nature. But if the Son is said to have been born from elsewhere, either his origin is asserted to be from nothing, or (as was said above) it is proclaimed, against the rule of true faith, that something besides God has always existed. Indeed the blessed Apostle, knowing that the Son was begotten true God from the essence of the Father, and for this reason one Lord God with the Father, and not forgetful of the Lord's precept by which we are forbidden to serve two masters, commanded that the Lord Christ be served as true God, whom he knew must be honoured equally with the Father, as the Lord himself says: That all may honour the Son as they honour the Father (John 5:23). John the apostle, the Lord himself speaking in him, testifies that he is true God, saying: That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ; this is the true God and eternal life (1 John 5:20). Therefore the rule of true faith must be held, by which the Son of God is believed to have been born ineffably, without beginning, from the substance of the Father, that is, from that which he himself is, and is worshipped and held (another reading: feared) as true God with the Father. For it is neither lawful for Christians to serve as true God one who is not God by nature, nor is it right for anyone not to serve Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, as true God. For blessed Paul, who had forbidden service to gods (another reading: to these) that are not gods by nature, shows most plainly that he who serves Christ pleases God, saying: The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but justice and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit: for whoever serves Christ in this pleases God (Rom. 14:17-18). Therefore, recognising that Christ is true God, let us not dare to separate him from equality with the paternal substance: for he is true God who is God by nature; and he is God by nature who has had deity from eternity by true birth, not possessed it by a gift of grace. For what is born is joined by kind; but what is adopted is advanced by generosity alone.

Objection 5. The disturbances of minds which are spoken without reason, when they urge attention, the truth does not seem to be grasped by them, nor professed, because it is absurd to say or believe that the Father and the Son are unbegotten. Whoever persuades himself to devise these things wishes to deceive himself by a fraud, which indeed requires this to be said to those who assert that the Father and the Son are equal.

Answer. Those who would call the Father and the Son unbegotten do indeed disturb minds, whether sluggish or ignorant; but those who are known to proclaim the Father and the Son equal do not do this. For in two unbegotten [beings] a divided Godhead is found. But in one begotten (another reading: one Only-begotten) from one unbegotten, a natural unity is shown. For two unbegotten [beings] cannot have one nature, where neither does one find in the other a true generation from himself, nor does one truly recognise in himself a substance of birth from the other. We, however, neither call the Father and the Son two unbegotten, nor name them two begotten, nor confound them in person, nor separate them in substance. And therefore we call them equal without ambiguity, because we find them in no way different from each other: one begot one, one was born from one. And because an unchangeable Son came forth from an unchangeable Father, and the eternal and perfect Father begot a coeternal and perfect Son, therefore the Son could have neither a lesser nor a different substance from that true one which he has from the true Father. For it is an insult to the divine nature if the Father, begetting the Son, could not be in the Son as great as he remains in himself; and natural power is taken from the begetter (which it is wicked to think) if equality of the paternal substance is denied to the Son, since the apostolic teaching does not pass this over in silence, as John the evangelist says: For this reason the Jews wanted to kill him, because he not only broke the sabbath, but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God (John 5:18). This equality was not alleged by the malevolent hostility of the Jews (as it seems to some), but was declared by the wholly truthful authority of the evangelist. Just as he truly said that Jesus broke the sabbath, and truly that he called God his Father, so he truly said that through professing the name of Father he made himself equal to the divinity and omnipotence of the begetter. Proclaiming and showing this equality in himself, the true Son says: I and the Father are one (John 10:30). And in another place: Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise (John 5:19). He himself says: Father, glorify your Son, that the Son also may glorify you (John 17:1). And in another place: That all may honour the Son as they honour the Father (John 5:23). And many other things, which we have omitted to avoid prolixity. So to make himself equal to God through professing the name of Father, to be one with the Father, to do likewise the same things that the Father does, to be glorified and himself to glorify, to claim for himself equality of the Father's honour: just as these do not befit one who is lesser, so they show him equal, every scruple of doubt removed.

Objection 6. Meanwhile, when light is spoken of, they do not understand what is written: that the Father of light is one, and another is he who is called light, and shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not grasp him. Therefore one must take note of what the law commands, or how it instructs the minds of men: that between that author of light and this light shining in the darkness, which enlightens every man coming into this world, through which the Son was made life and was shown to be the light of men, being made that which is shown, he is not the Father, and cannot be equal.

Reply. The equality of the Father and the Son always shows this: that whatever there is of disparagement or of honour is common to both together. Hence it comes about that, when against the rule of faith the Son is set apart from equality with the Father, it is the Father rather than the Son who is disparaged. The assertion in this passage shows this more plainly: for while the Son alone is believed to be called light, the name of light is denied to the Father himself, who begot the light. But he who does not possess the name of light substantially cannot have the title of Deity substantially. For blessed John the apostle says: For God is light (1 John 1:5). If, then, he who is God is light, he who is not light is not God; therefore the Son must be believed to be light from light, because he is God born of God, lest, while the Son is called light, God the Father be intolerably blasphemed. And lest we be thought to call the Father light by conjecture rather than by truth, we must prove this too by testimonies. In the holy oracles it is said of Wisdom: Wisdom is more mobile than all mobile things (another reading: than all movable things, or than all motions); and she reaches everywhere because of her purity; for she is a vapour of the power of God, and a certain pure emanation of the glory of almighty God. And therefore nothing defiled enters into her; for she is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God's majesty, and the image of his goodness. Wisdom is called the brightness of eternal light, and all Christendom professes that this eternal light is the Father. But if perhaps some think that this eternal light, whose brightness Wisdom is, ought not to be taken as the Father, then, while they deny that God the Father is eternal light, they must seek another eternal light, and show plainly that Wisdom is its brightness. But let them see how they can find either a light that is not God, or another light, besides Wisdom, that is coeternal with God. Let the Father of light, then, be recognised as light, so that at least in this way the Son may not be doubted or denied to be equal to the Father. Having already taught by one testimony that God the Father is light, it is better if we show the same thing by apostolic preaching as well. Blessed Paul testifies that we are sons of God, saying: Whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God: for you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the spirit of adoption of sons, in which we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God (Rom. 8:14-16). John the evangelist also says: But as many as believed in him, he gave them power to become sons of God (John 1:12). So, in order to show that God, whose sons we are, is light, Paul called these same sons also sons of light, saying thus: But you, brothers, are not in darkness, that that day should overtake you like a thief; for you are all sons of light and sons of the day (1 Thess. 5:4-5). And the Son [says] to the disciples: That you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:45). That the Son himself is light no one can deny, of whom the evangelist says: He was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world (John 1:9). And again: And the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not grasp it (ibid., 4-5). The Son himself also testifies with his own voice that he is light, saying: I am the light of the world (John 8:12). And that the Father may be recognised to be in the Son, light in light, is fully taught in the testimony of John, who says: God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all; and he added: If we walk in the light, as he too is in the light, we have fellowship with one another (1 John 1:5, 7). And to show that he had said this of the Father, he added: And the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (ibid., 7). The Father, whom he called light, he declared to be in the light. What then is this light, if not the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world (John 1:9)? It has therefore been shown that the Father is light, as the Son is light; and the Son is also shown to be day, as the Father too is day, since the prophet says: Announce his salvation from day to day (Ps. 95:2). Therefore let the Father be recognised to be in the Son, the light, and the Son in the Father, the light, as the light itself declares concerning itself: I in the Father, and the Father in me (John 14:10-11); as if he were saying: I in the light, and the light in me. And where no difference of light is found, let equality of deity not be denied: lest, while God is said by apostolic preaching to be light, he who is not said to be light should also be denied (which is unlawful) to be God.

Objection 7. We have omitted (another reading: admitted, or lost) superfluous reasonings, so that they should not cause weariness to the hearers, and a reply has been given to that for which the statement sought an explanation. And since there is a distance between the Father and the Son, and what is said, that there is no difference between them, is not so, the Saviour himself, who must be believed, says: There is another who bears witness about me (John 5:32). Likewise the Son himself says of the Holy Spirit: And I will send you another Paraclete (John 14:16). He called the Father another, and he called the Paraclete another; and when divine laws and sacraments are not heeded, men become professors of paganism, when they assert that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God.

Reply. The true faith never has nor had superfluous reasonings, but always right ones; nor does any weariness arise from them, provided the truth is heard without zeal for contention. The truth called the Father another for this reason, to distinguish the persons, not to show a distance of substance: for when he said another, he showed that he has his own person; but in naming him Father, he showed that he has one substance with him, in this way: if the Father, who bears witness to the Son, is truly another, so that the person of each is distinguished, he is also truly Father, so that unity of substance is shown. And if the fatherhood of the Father is true, the birth of the offspring is also true; and if the birth of the Son is true, there can be no difference of substance between the Father and the Son. For the true and eternal substance, from which the true birth came forth, just as it could not be diminished or divided by begetting, so, remaining whole in itself, it gave itself whole to the coeternal truth of the birth, so that not only should there be equality of begetter and begotten without difference, but also the unity of nature should remain without confusion or loss. For both the name and the truth of the divine birth, just as they show the person of the begetter and the begotten as distinct, so they do not allow the substance to be thought different. The Father, then, was called another for this reason, that the truth of the generation might be shown, not that he might be thought either prior or superior: for if we must take him whom we hear called another as superior, we are compelled also to confess the Paraclete Spirit, because he was called another, superior to the Son: for just as the Son called the Father another, so he named the Paraclete another. If, then, it pleases, and the truth of faith demands this, that he who is called another be thought better, since the Father was called another, and the Paraclete another, then let the Son now be subjected to both, so that at least in this way the Paraclete may be made equal to the Father, since he is said to be placed before the Son because he was named another; so that by sharing this pronoun a sharing of deity may be shown in the Father and the Paraclete. But if the Paraclete, although he is called another, is nevertheless not preferred to the Son, neither is the Father to be preferred to the Son because he is called another: for by this pronoun a distinction of persons is shown, not of nature. Finally, lest through the ambiguity of faith we abandon the rule of truth and be carried about through wandering errors, the Lord himself showed us both that he keeps one substance with the Father and that he has a different person, saying in the Gospel: I and the Father are one (John 10:30). This saying those who strive to weaken the meaning of divine unity in the Father and the Son are eager to refer not to unity of substance but to harmony of will. But if the Lord wished to be understood so, he could have said: I and the Father will one thing; not: I and the Father are one. But now let each choose what he wishes: whether he thinks that in God to be is one thing and to will another, or believes that to be is the same as to will, so that the truth of this saying of the Lord may appear to him more plainly. For if he says that in God the will, which is called willing, is one thing, and the essence, which is known as being, another, then what was said according to essence cannot be referred to will: I and the Father are one. For to be is named from essence. But if in God (as is certain) to be is held to be the same as to will, then while unity of will is asserted, let unity of substance not be denied either; so that in his saying one it may be recognised that he is nothing other than what the Father is, and in his saying are it may be recognised that the Son himself is not he who is the Father. Following this teaching of Christ in all things, our Fathers said that the Father and the Son are of one substance. This was called in Greek Homousion, for the reason, namely, that a new heresy had then arisen among the Greeks which strove to separate the Only-begotten from the substance of the begetter, so that whoever received that teaching would appear a worshipper not of the creator but rather of a creature. But it is strange that in this term some attend only to the sound and do not search out the meaning of what is said, since many things were not said in ancient times, and are found inserted into the profession of faith according to the needs of times and circumstances. Thus unbegotten Father is nowhere read in the canonical Scriptures, and yet according to the truth of faith he is proclaimed unbegotten: namely against Sabellius, who understands the Father and the Son as one not by communion of substance but confuses them by singleness of person. But if the sound and not the sense is considered in words, let the Church not be designated by the name Catholic, which is found set down in neither the Old nor the New Testament. But if all these things, though they are in no canonical book, are nevertheless rightly held in faith, why should it be thought forbidden to us, in Homousion, to consider not the sound of the word but the sense, and not to attend to the novelty of the word but to understand the force of the mystery? And it is strange that those who wish us to be called Homousians because of our belief in one substance are unwilling themselves to be called Triusians, because of three and different substances; although, even if they shun being designated by such a name, the character of their belief shows that this is what they are. Rightly, therefore, keeping the distinctness of persons, we worship the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit as one God; for the true faith neither accepts three gods, as the pagans who worship many do, nor asserts that its God was created, as the worshippers of a creature proclaim.

Objection 8. Let men who desire to follow saving precepts take note that it is a crime and very blasphemous: for falsity of profession will never be able to profit those who seek to worship or venerate God by insulting [him] through blasphemy. If an insult is not tolerated by men, how could it be tolerated by the Lord, the author himself? For he shows his rebuke towards unbelievers, saying: This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me (Isa. 29:13).

Reply. The apostolic faith does not insult God but honours him, for it asserts that the divine substance could neither be diminished nor changed; and for that reason it proclaims the Son equal to the Father, since the one substance of both keeps the fullness of its perfection in each. An insult is offered to God, then, when through a difference of divinity the creation is worshipped together with the Creator; whereas the name of creation is to be accepted in the Son only in this, that for the redemption of men he was made man from men. The Holy Spirit too, if the Lord wished him to be understood as a creature, he would never have commanded to be joined to himself and the Father in the sacrament of baptism, saying: Go, teach all nations, baptising (another reading: baptise) them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19).

Objection 9. Concerning his generation, as for what was said: From the womb before the morning star I begot you (Ps. 109:3), who would doubt that it was said of the fleshly birth? For the writing itself shows you beforehand, so that you may understand what the prophet says, that he was begotten in the brightness of the saints before the morning star. And the brightness of the saints (ibid.) is shown to be the proclamation of the prophets, and their prophecy about him to have been fulfilled, so that it should make plain that it was so, the prophet too saying: From the womb before the morning star I begot you; and it came about splendidly, that he should be born through a virgin, as the prophetic mouth had said before. Who would doubt that this birth came about just as Scripture records?

Reply. He is much deceived who does not believe that this passage of Scripture fits the divine birth, and who, hearing that God said: From the womb before the morning star I begot you, because a fleshly womb cannot be believed to be in God, thinks that the sense of this passage must be fitted only to that generation which is according to the flesh; whereas the preceding verse rather suggests the understanding of the divine generation, in which the Father says to the Son: With you is the beginning (ibid.), so that the Father and the Son may be recognised to be one beginning. The name of womb, however, was used as a transferred term, by which the divine nature itself should be signified; just as the incorporeal substance of God is customarily named by bodily names, so that the minds of men may be led by the familiar words of their own nature to an understanding of the divinity. For the eyes of God are said to see all things, as it is written: In every place the eyes of God watch the good and the evil (Prov. 15:3). But who would doubt that God sees everything through his nature in such a way as we confess that he fills all things through the infinity of his nature? But we also find the various names of bodily members used of God for this reason (as has been said), that through the workings of these things the distinct character of his incorporeal substance may be understood. So here too, then, he said that he begot the Son from the womb, so that no one should think him whom we hear to have been begotten from the womb a stranger to the nature of the Father. And by saying before the morning star, he showed that the everlasting birth of the Son is not subject to a beginning in time: for 'morning star' is the name of a star, and at the beginning of the world, when God had made the lights and the stars, he commanded them to serve for days, and months, and times, and years (Gen. 1:14), by which cycles of names all time revolves. But by in the brightness of the saints the prophecies of the prophets have not been rightly understood: for the brightness of the saints consists not in the office of preaching but in the glory of the resurrection; of which brightness the Lord says: Then the just will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. 13:43). This brightness of the future resurrection the prophet Daniel also records in these words: And many of those who sleep in the pit of the earth, in the covering, will rise, these to eternal life, and these to reproach and everlasting confusion; and those who understand will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and many of the just like the stars for ever (Dan. 12:2-3); and this brightness will be granted to the saints by the Lord at the time when, according to the Apostle's saying, he will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory (Phil. 3:21). In this brightness, then, the saints will fully understand that the Father and the Son are one beginning, and do not differ from one another either in substance or in majesty. Although, then, we confess that the Son according to the flesh was brought forth from the womb of the Virgin, we nevertheless do not doubt that he was begotten from the womb of the Father, that is, from the substance of the Father; indeed we confess that the Son was born true God from the womb of God just as we do not doubt that he came forth true man from the womb of the Virgin; lest (God forbid) if true man is believed to have been born from the substance of the mother, and true God is denied [to have been born] from the substance of the Father, human nature, which could bring forth what it is, should be thought stronger than the divine substance, which was not able to beget true God.

Objection 10. It is no small (another reading: no excessive) disgrace that an ill-understanding mind should be deceived by its own frauds, so that sometimes two are said to be one, sometimes three one. Does the gift of a benefit not present itself, when one is not designated together with two? It is a mockery to believe that one God consists of three parts, when moreover (what is worse) it is said of them that one God is to be believed in this way, though the Father is not the same as the Son, nor the Son the same as the Holy Spirit; of whom they profess that they have differences among themselves, but that each cannot have his own honour unless a malicious heart is found to join them together in one God.

Reply. He is deceived by no frauds, either his own or another's, who so worships one God that he knows, in the Trinity, neither to confuse the persons nor to separate the substance. And he understands as one God that one nature in which he recognises the eternity of true divinity; for it is said to us: Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord (Deut. 6:4). Likewise: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve (ibid., 13). But if we ought to take the Father alone as the Lord God, then we should neither serve the Son as God nor worship him; for whatever does not belong to the nature of the Lord God alone ought not to be worshipped by us as God. But what shall we say of the Son, whom the angels and all the powers in heaven always worship and praise, so much so that even when he was set in the form of a servant, and on account of the suffering of death made a little lower than the angels, the angels are commanded to worship him, as Moses says: Rejoice, you heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God worship him (Ps. 96:7)? David too, divinely inspired, adding men to this worship, says: All the kings of the earth will worship him, all nations serve (another reading: will serve) him (Ps. 71:11). How then is he worshipped both by men and by angels, if he is separated from the substance of the one God? How do we dare to show him the service which is owed to God alone, if he does not have one nature with the Father? For since God is one, it is said to us thus through the prophet: I am God, and there is no other besides me: just and saving, and there is no other besides me: turn to me and you will be saved, for from the end of the earth I am God, and there is no other. By myself I swear, that justice will go out (another reading: went out) from my mouth, and my words will not be turned back: for to me the whole world will bend (another reading: bent) the knee, and every tongue will swear (another reading: swore) by God (Isa. 45:21 ff.). See, God, who in this place, calling himself alone God, testifies that there is no other besides him. But if anyone is unwilling to take the whole Trinity here, he will be forced to assign this utterance to the Son alone. For who is the God besides whom there is no other, if not he to whom Isaiah says: Egypt has laboured, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabaeans (another reading: Saba), tall men, will pass over to you, they will be servants, and will follow after you bound in chains, and will worship you, and will make supplication in you, since God is in you, and there is no God besides you; for you are God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Saviour. All who oppose him will blush and be ashamed, and will go in confusion (ibid., 14 ff.). See, God is in him, and besides him there is no God, and he is the God of Israel, the Saviour. And above, he who said: I am God, and there is no other besides me, added: Just and saving, there is no other besides me. But who is just, if not he to whom David says: You have loved justice and hated iniquity (Ps. 44:8)? And who is saving, if not he of whom the angel spoke to Joseph in sleep, saying: Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for what is born in her is of the Holy Spirit: and she will bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus; for he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:20-21)? And whom does it befit to say: Turn to me and you will be saved, for from the end of the earth I am God, and there is no other (Isa. 45:22), if not the Son? Of whom David says: All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the homelands of the nations will worship in his sight (Ps. 21:28). As for what follows, then: By myself I swear, who is to be believed to say this, if not he who is found to have sworn in this way to Abraham before? And they assert that this was not the Father but the Son, who strive to proclaim the Son lesser than the Father according to the divine nature. But whether this God, who swears by himself, has anyone greater than himself, blessed Paul shows us, who, writing to the Hebrews, says: For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying: Surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you (Heb. 6:13-14). This God, then, who swears by himself since he has no one greater by whom to swear: let us see what follows: For justice, he says, will go out from my mouth, and my words will not be turned back: for to me the whole world will bend (another reading: bent) the knee, and every tongue will swear (another reading: swore) by God (Isa. 45:23). From whose mouth, then, did justice go out, if not from his of whom Isaiah said: A rod will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise up from his root, and the spirit of the Lord will rest upon him (Isa. 11:1-2)? And a little after: He will judge the poor in justice, and will reprove the earth (another reading: for the meek of the earth) in equity for the meek (ibid., 4). Then follows: This God, besides whom there is no other, also says: My words will not be turned back. And whose utterance is this, if not his who says in the Gospel: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Matt. 24:35)? Likewise this God, besides whom there is no other, adds and says: For to me the whole world will bend (another reading: bent) the knee, and every tongue will swear (another reading: swore) by God. And of whom this ought to be understood Paul, taught by the instruction of Christ, shows us, who, writing to the Romans, speaks thus: For none of us lives for himself, and none dies for himself. For if we live, we live for the Lord; if we die, we die for the Lord. Whether then we live or die, we are the Lord's (Rom. 14:7-8). And to show that he had said this of Christ, he added: For to this end Christ both died and rose again, that he might be Lord of the dead and of the living. But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgement seat of God (Rom. 14:9-10). And at once he adds this prophetic testimony, saying: For it is written: As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God (Isa. 45:24). And that we shall stand (another reading: shall be set) before the judgement seat of Christ he himself testifies again, saying: For we must all be made manifest before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each may receive the things proper to the body, according as he has done, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10). The same apostle also teaches that every knee must bow to him, saying: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth, and below the earth; and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:10-11). Now let us consider again all the things that have been said above. God says: I am God, and there is no other besides me. And in the person of the Son Isaiah says: For God is in you, and besides you there is no God; for you are God, and we did not know [it], God of Israel, Saviour (Isa. 45:15). But the God of Israel is one God. And there follow the other things which we have shown by the testimonies above to pertain to the Son: for he swears by himself, having no one greater; he saves his people; he judges justly; to him every knee bows, of things in heaven, on earth, and below the earth; to him every tongue confesses, by whom the recompense of deeds is to be rendered. He, then, of whom all these things are said, says through the prophet: I am God, and there is no other besides me. Do we then take this God, besides whom there is no other, to be the Son alone, in such a way that we separate the Father and the Holy Spirit from him? God forbid: for this is impossible. For besides God the Father there is no God the Son, because he is from the Father and is in the Father. Besides the Father and the Son there is no Holy Spirit, because he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, and is in the Father and in the Son. From this it is recognised that this Trinity is one Lord God, of whom it is said: Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord (another reading: God) is one (Deut. 6:4). And: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve. To this Lord the prophet Isaiah also says: Lord, besides you we know no other, we name your name. This name our Saviour shows, saying to his disciples: Go, teach all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19). This is the name of the Lord, besides whom we know no other, and by the naming of whose name we are freed from death and rescued from the power of darkness, so that we may be transferred into the kingdom of the Son. In the Father, then, and the Son and the Holy Spirit we accept a unity of substance; we do not dare to confuse the persons. For the blessed apostle John testifies, saying: There are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and the three are one (1 John 5:7). This the most blessed martyr Cyprian also confesses in his letter On the Unity of the Church, saying: He who breaks the peace and concord of Christ acts against Christ; he who gathers elsewhere than in the Church scatters the Church of Christ. And to show that the one Church belongs to the one God, he at once inserted these testimonies from the Scriptures: The Lord says: I and the Father are one. And again: Of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit it is written: And the three are one. For also in his book On the Lord's Prayer, to show that the Trinity is of one deity and has no diversity among its members, he recalled that Daniel and the three youths were accustomed to pour out prayer when cycles of three hours had come round. There, both in the course of three hours and in the offering of one prayer, he plainly shows that the Trinity is one God. We do not, then, worship one God made of three parts; but, holding to the rule of the apostolic faith, we confess the Son, perfect and co-eternal, begotten without beginning from the perfect and eternal Father, not unequal in power and equal in nature. The Holy Spirit too we confess to be nothing other than God, neither different from the Son nor from the Father, nor confused in the Son or in the Father. For the Spirit of the Father and of the Son is one and the same, proceeding wholly from the Father, abiding wholly in both; nor is he divided between them singly, since he is inseparably common to both.
